summary: This Wikipedia article on the color red traces its cultural and symbolic meanings across history. It covers red in Communist and Pan-Slavic flags, Renaissance and later painting pigments such as carmine, medieval and Byzantine royal and religious uses, its role as a revolutionary symbol during the French Revolution, its artistic use in the 19th century including Van Gogh, and its association with courage, martyrdom and sacrifice.
one_line: Wikipedia overview of red's symbolic, political, religious and artistic meanings across history, from flags and pigments to revolution and martyrdom.
key_facts: After the Communist Party of China took power in 1949, the Chinese flag became a red flag with a large star symbolizing the Communist Party.
Carmine, made from cochineal, gave painters a very fine crimson but tended to change color if not used carefully.
Rembrandt, Vermeer, Rubens, Anthony van Dyck, Diego Velázquez and Tintoretto were among the great 15th and 16th century painters who used carmine.
Red, blue, and white were the Pan-Slavic colors adopted by the Slavic solidarity movement of the late nineteenth century.
In 2004 Georgia adopted a new white flag with four small red crosses and one big red cross in the middle.
In the early 12th century, Abbe Suger added stained glass windows with blue cobalt glass and red glass tinted with copper to Saint Denis Basilica outside Paris.
Beginning in 1295, Roman Catholic cardinals began to wear red costumes.
The Party anthem of the Communist Party of China under Mao Zedong became "The East Is Red".
The sayings of Mao Zedong were published as a small red book in hundreds of millions of copies during the Cultural Revolution.
During the French Revolution, the Jacobins and other radical parties used red as a symbol of liberty and personal freedom.
Women wearing red caps gathered around the guillotine to celebrate each execution during the Reign of Terror; they were called the "Furies of the guillotine".
After the Reign of Terror, France returned to the blue, white and red tricolor, whose red was taken from the traditional color of Saint Denis.
Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo in 1888 that he "sought to express with red and green the terrible human passions" in The Night Cafe.
Surveys show that red is the color most associated with courage.
The banner of the Christian soldiers in the First Crusade was a red cross on a white field, the St. George's Cross.
The Saint George's Cross became the Flag of England in the 16th century and is now part of the Union Flag of the United Kingdom.
